body.text: There is a paradox in the AI industry today: while power-hungry data centres are shaping and accelerating the development of the renewables industry, the industry remains sensitive to government decisions. It booms when governments pour subsidies to lower the cost of development and adoption; conversely, it will encounter a bust when governments roll them back.

In Malaysia, renewables follow the same pattern of government dependency. Although the country first named renewable energy as the ‘fifth fuel’ a quarter of a century ago, its key renewable, solar, only grew in incremental steps. Each increment was determined by the quotas for how much solar capacity could be built and sold, or auction rounds the government allocated. An underlying structural barrier limited the industry’s growth. Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB), the national utility, has consistently been the sole buyer of electricity, primarily procured from coal and gas plants under long-term contracts. Demand did not grow as fast as supply over the years; in 2019, the grid had a huge reserve margin of more than 30 per cent. In this context, every new megawatt of solar energy is competing with existing energy supplies. The government and TNB thus kept solar quotas low and bought solar at the lowest bids.

There was a change in this situation in 2023, when the government introduced the National Energy Transition Roadmap, which raised the country’s renewables target to an ambitious 70 per cent of its total power mix. The 2025 level was 32 per cent. The old approach of rationed growth no longer worked. A series of policy reforms to open up the market followed. The roadmap includes lifting the export ban on renewables, enabling third-party grid access, retiring coal-fired plants in phases and launching the Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS). The latter allowed companies to buy green power directly from a renewable energy supplier instead of only from TNB.

Data centres made this possible because it was an entirely new category of growth. An AI data centre today is 10 to 100 times larger than an average pre-AI data centre. Solar developers can sell directly to data centres willing to pay a premium for fast access to large amounts of electricity. From July 2025, data centres paid a separate ultra-high voltage tariff from standard residential and industrial rates. TNB also benefited by collecting grid fees for this new source of electricity. The scale was unlike anything before. By June 2026, data centres had booked 8.35 gigawatts (GW) from TNB. This is more than a third of West Malaysia’s record peak demand, and nearly as much as Singapore’s peak demand of 8.6 GW in August 2026.
Renewables are now enjoying an upward spiral due to data centre energy demand, but a reversal into a downward spiral remains a real and overlooked risk.

This led to a virtuous cycle: energy availability attracts data centre investors, and these centres in turn spurred the energy industry to build more capacity. In this context, renewables are attractive because they are relatively faster to build and help meet the emissions targets of global data centre companies. The adjustment of renewables access charges and the government mandate for data centres to procure at least 30 per cent of their energy from renewables will help to spur the industry. The latter is estimated to unlock up to MYR36 billion of opportunities in renewable energy, according to analysts. Thus far, Malaysia’s installed renewable energy capacity stands at 32 per cent, slightly ahead of its 31 per cent target for 2025.

Google has signed major long-term deals with Shizen Energy and TotalEnergies to supply solar power for its data centres, and intends to take up 1 GW of renewables under CRESS. Blue chip conglomerates SD Guthrie and Gamuda Engineering have also been contracted to supply up to 680 megawatts (MW) of renewable energy to a US multinational’s data centre project. Public listed companies in the renewables industry — including Solarvest, Samaiden and the Pekat Group — were major beneficiaries of these policies and events. Solarvest, in particular, was a standout. In the financial year ended March 2026, its revenue increased 41 per cent and net profit jumped 54 per cent compared to the previous year. Its stock price has increased by 167 per cent since 2023.

The largest Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) investments also came from data centres, which require 24/7 electricity. BESS, which uses networks of batteries to store electricity, addresses the issue of solar intermittency, especially at night, and is fast to build. Data centre provider DayOne’s agreement with TNB included a 2.2 gigawatt-hour (GWh) BESS, the largest known investment of its kind.

That said, however, having data centres as a major growth driver carries significant risks. Globally, spending on data centre infrastructure is estimated to be among the largest and fastest-growing investments in history; it is also heavily leveraged. Building renewable infrastructure and upgrading the grid (MYR 43 billion) to cater for this demand carries the risk of stranded assets if the global AI bet does not pay off. While these assets could theoretically be used to cater to alternative demand, it would be difficult to find other demand sources that are as big as data centres. Data centres’ intense energy demand may also have the opposite effect of not meeting renewables targets if all sources, including non-renewable sources, are activated, such as reviving coal-fired plants from planned retirement. At the same time, the wider economic spillover from the renewables industry — such as manufacturing linkages, skilled employment, technology and R&D — remains unknown, as most equipment is still imported wholesale from countries like China.

The bullish attitude of the Malaysian government toward data centres since 2023 has understandably turned cautious over the past year. One-third of data centre applications in the Johor state were rejected in 2024, with recent ones put on hold. Some approved applications are scrutinised for genuine demand; and stricter conditions are set on efficiency and offtaking, where a buyer pays for a set amount of energy even if it uses less. This new approach is warranted given the growing concerns about the scale of AI infrastructure spending. Renewables are now enjoying an upward spiral due to data centre energy demand, but a reversal into a downward spiral remains a real and overlooked risk.
